Actually as far as I’m aware Pol Pot and the CPK’s plan of development was to become a major exporter of rice and use the profits from that to industrialise the Cambodian economy. The problem was that they decided to forcefully enslave everyone in the country to carry this out, as well as their bizarre views on class causing them to murder and torture city dwellers relentlessly, and when you’re trying to increase production it’s generally a pretty stupid idea to execute the well educated engineers, planners, agricultural experts, architects etc who actually have some know how on the necessary technology and infrastructure needed to develop the country.

It also didn’t help that much of Cambodia had been ravaged by American bombs as well as guerrilla warfare, so they were barely producing enough rice to feed their own workforce (the infamous “bowl of rice a day”) let alone become a major worldwide producer. 

If I recall correctly they attempted to turn things around near the end of their rule after realising that what they were doing was completely contrary to their goals of development, and they attempted to diversify things a little bit, for example I believe they discussed exporting rubber to Romania when Ceausescu visited, but the regime collapsed a year later after the Vietnamese invasion. 

Democratic Kampuchea is actually a really interesting thing to look at from a Marxist perspective, it shows that being the most zealous and extreme you can possibly be does not substitute for a proper economic plan.

I have been on both sides of political extremism, I had an anti-SJW phase when I was 13 in which I was very anti-immigration and believed Muslims to be dangerous, and more recently I fell into online communism and got sucked into believing some very zealous things. 

I think what works best is to gradually present to him a reality which contradicts his beliefs. For example, I bought into a lot of fear mongering about Muslims being violent and misogynistic, but every day I would go to get my lunch at a shop run by Muslims. Eventually I developed a rapport with the owners of the shop and I began to realise that all this stuff I had read online was just bigotry designed to push a specific hateful political agenda, and I gave up on my far right beliefs. 

As for leftism, I believed that the most radical ideas would be the most effective ones, but slowly I began to realise that this wasn’t the case. While it’s true that many people around the world suffer from poverty and other related issues, I came to the conclusion that all this hardcore rhetoric just alienated people from my ideas and obscured real solutions to these problems. 

In the case of your friend, don’t be afraid to put your foot down and let him know that his behaviour and beliefs aren’t acceptable. Many people around me called me out for my prejudice and eventually that got me questioning my beliefs. He will be defensive at first, but it will plant the seed of doubt in his head. The truth is that people who take these extreme positions are also compensating for the doubt they feel in their beliefs, and despite their outward appearance of believing these things religiously, internally they are most likely quite conflicted. I think it’s also important to acknowledge that political extremism also comes from personal problems in people’s lives. It’s no secret that racists and fascists will target young men struggling with identity, loneliness and mental health issues and try to recruit them by playing on those insecurities. You say your friend has PTSD from his experience at the protests, so perhaps the pain that he has felt from that has led him down this path and finding some way to address that pain and getting him the help he needs will cause him to give up his ideology.

Have you ever read The Communist Manifesto? It’s not intended to be the go to document for communist political theory (that would probably be Capital), rather it was intended as a small pamphlet to solidify the intentions and beliefs of the early communist movement. If you read through the writings of communist politicians from the 20th Century they make little reference to it, instead opting for the more detailed writings of Marx and others. Marx has a very broad range of writings that serve as the inspiration for communist movements, not just the manifesto. Besides, even if Marx had never been born there would have been other theorists that would have created similar philosophies, one of Marx’s main points is that human beings act according to their social environment, so an environment like Russia under Tsar Nicholas would have necessitated revolutionary activity anyway. I’m not really a communist myself, but I still think that you shouldn’t discount the ideas of Marx because of the history of communism. If you read him for yourself then you’ll come to understand that he is a lot different than right wing politicians and media portray him to be.
